This was a bit of a journey of a read. Unusually for me, I stopped reading part-way through and switched to Murderbot, because I was just finding it a bit slow and unengaging and needed something a bit more comforting. The beginning just didn't grab me, both in terms of writing style generally and the plot, and I was a bit worried it'd be a kind of 2/5 read that I may not actually finish. I'd not read anything by the author before, and I'm not sure what's their style vs what's intentionally written in a bit of a jarring and clunky way because of how the main character is.

On putting down Murderbot I took this up again, and slowly it started to connect a bit more. I went through a moment where it felt a bit like when I read Ninefox Gambit, which didn't fully click with me but then I really liked the sequels. The premise of arcspace and its... challenges... is actually very interesting (even if - light spoilers - it never actually gets fully explained or resolved). There had been a lot of care put into the details about the different societies and cultures, with them all having very clear, fully-fleshed out personalities and uniqueness. I really enjoyed this side of the book, and on learning more about the others, it did put some of the earlier Shine backstory slowness into some better context.

That said, there's a lot of what felt to me somewhat unnecessary extra details around the edges, and a good chunk of the book feels like episodic, particularly with jumping forward considerable chunks of time. One chapter ends "and that was how I met X and Y" (paraphrasing) to set up the next one, which feels like they should be consequential, but end up as a (literally) very short lived interaction. There's quite a bit of that around the edges of the main threads, and whilst it all comes together quite rapidly right at the end, it never quite got to the "wow" stage.

So, the good: interesting concepts overall, some nice details around cultures and settings, great characterisation, a story that was interesting once it got going. But set against some slow and somewhat clunky writing in parts (a chapter almost all in caps was also not fun to read on a practical level), pacing being a bit off, some unsatisfying open threads that could have done with a bit more payoff.
